items.title: From Intent to Effect: 639 Proposed Direction for AI Safety and 48-Stage Workflows for Three-Valued Operational Consistency in AI-Driven Infrastructure
items.abstract: Autonomous and AI-driven systems now issue operations whose consequences land far from where they were decided: in radio-access-network controllers, operator charging systems, device queues and DMA engines, robot actuators, emergency broadcast channels, payment rails, browsers, and long-running agent processes that migrate between hosts. Across all of these, a recurring failure appears. A system treats an acknowledgement, a status code, a callback, a log entry, or its own internal view as if it were proof that the intended effect occurred, on the intended target, under the conditions that were authorized. Observations are fused across mismatched clocks, identities, and configuration generations; agreements are treated as execution authority; partial effects are retried as if nothing happened; translated or transformed instructions are delivered as though they preserved their original meaning. This disclosure addresses that gap as a single architectural problem expressed across many domains. The disclosure presents a 280-page technical record comprising common-workflow flowcharts, phase-level engineering figures, implementation flowcharts, and 639 proposed patent claims. Its unifying principle is that the original authorized operation retains a stable identity from which every downstream representation, transformation, dispatch, acknowledgement, and observed effect must be separately reconstructed and qualified. Each workflow applies a conservative three-valued rule at every gate: all mandatory predicates supported advances; any predicate contradicted inhibits or raises an exception; any predicate unresolved holds. Final outcomes are expressed as scoped verdicts (CONSISTENT, INCONSISTENT, or UNRESOLVED) with the evidence, resource state, and gaps on which each verdict depends. Throughout, acknowledgement is distinguished from effect, observation from authority, eligibility from authorization, and historical records from current permission. The record is organized into technical groups, each with its own common workflow and claim set: Group A (claims 1–40) governs observation-to-control consistency in radio-access-network calculations: reconstructing resource identity and configuration generation, bounding temporal applicability under clock uncertainty, preserving measurement semantics across interfaces, selecting dependency-aware joint observations, maintaining consistency through controller migration and failover, and revalidating material dependencies before a control result is delivered. Group B (claims 41–80) addresses multi-agent network incident diagnosis and repair, covering source-qualified evidence provenance and independence, competing fault hypotheses resolved by discriminating evidence, repair-plan applicability under concurrent changes, asynchronous repair with partial-effect reconstruction, independent post-repair verification of recovery and adverse effects, and distributed incident history with recurrence analysis. Group C (claims 81–120) maintains telecommunications session lifecycle consistency across subscriber trust changes (SIM/eSIM), home and visited operator roaming and partial release, concurrent programmable quality-on-demand operations, user-plane usage, quota and charging lineage, purpose-scoped consent versus actual network effect, and partial operator outage with deferred settlement. Group D (claims 121–160) reconstructs hardware observation-to-effect consistency through independent hardware observers, CPU-to-device DMA memory continuity, device queue and descriptor occupancy, firmware and configuration invalidation, and cross-stage representation of external effects. Group E (claims 161–200) holds that negotiated agreement is not execution authority among multiple agents, covering versioned negotiation and partial acceptance, streaming artifacts and delegated sub-actions, amendment impact across versions, cancellation and late effects, partitioned participant views, and residual obligations at closure. Group F (claims 201–240) treats asynchronous tool and protocol operations, including durable task identity and callback origin, tool-schema generation and in-flight semantic change, acknowledged subscription and push-event coverage, resource alias and generation continuity, cancellation and retry with residual external effects, and concurrent usage-budget settlement. Group G (claims 241–280) translates machine-readable robot skills into calibration-qualified physical capability, evaluated by an independent safety controller, admitted under time-bounded command contracts, downgraded at runtime when capability degrades mid-actuation, transferred between robots without reusing unverified calibration, and closed by independent physical-effect observation. Group H (claims 281–320) carries emergency instructions from source to physical response: original instruction identity and provenance, extraction and preservation of safety-critical meaning, multilingual translation verification under uncertainty, recipient-specific exact-content dispatch, correction and supersession, and readback and response verification. Group M1 (claims 321–380) governs autonomous AI commerce from original purchase intent to actual commercial outcome, covering product, variant and seller continuity, complete monetary exposure at dynamic checkout, current purchasing authority, payment-mandate-to-financial-effect consistency, multi-agent shared budgets, and post-purchase fulfilment, refund, and correction. Group M2 (claims 381–440) operates at silicon level, binding an authorized operation to the hardware command a device actually consumes, through descriptor integrity, effective DMA translation and invalidation, reset and assignment incarnation, protected command admission with atomic use-state, shared quota admission, and cross-path effectuation coverage. Claims 441–509 extend the architecture to protected virtual-machine and sandbox runtimes with consequence-bound egress, dual-boundary digital-to-physical command enforcement, controller-local authority without transferable tokens, protected credential release, buffered physical-command invalidation, crash-resistant authority recovery, authority preservation across checkpoint, fork, migration and changing delegation, and separation of informative context from consequential execution. Group I (claims 510–539, with 600–639) secures browser and graphical-agent actions by binding an authorized task to the actual interface target, frame, origin, redirect, and background request it produces, and extends this to interface-independent control across graphical, voice, remote, native, and terminal interfaces. Group J (claims 540–599, with 600–639) preserves a persistent agent task’s logical identity, authority, outstanding external exposure, and callbacks across migration between execution instances, using generation fencing, representation-independent current authority, and callback-independent outcome verification, including treatment of partial and streaming effects without duplicate repetition. The material is offered as a public technical disclosure and reference architecture. The claims are proposed, not granted, and the figures describe implementation designs rather than guarantees of novelty, freedom to operate, or regulatory compliance. Safety-related content, including robotic and emergency-communication workflows, is non-certified and makes no SIL, PL, or standards-conformance claim. The record is intended for system architects, network and hardware engineers, AI-agent developers, standards contributors, and regulators concerned with accountable autonomy, where the question is not only whether an action was permitted, but whether what actually happened corresponds to what was authorized. items.title: From Narrative to Intent Schema Architecture: An Artificial Intelligence System for Human-Centered Advising Decision Support
items.abstract: Transfer advising is a high-uncertainty setting where students rarely ask well-structured questions and advisors must infer intent from fragmented narratives across conflicting institutional policies. This research presents a human-centered AI framework that transforms naturalistic student discourse into structured advising intents, supporting a student-facing advising assistant whose explainable outputs are designed to support advisor review. Using 19,668 transfer-related Reddit posts, it surfaces recurring advising intents via extraction, clustering, and structured labeling, then routes student questions to them. On a proof-of-concept benchmark it reached 90% intent-level and 86% question-level accuracy, turning advising knowledge into transparent structures that support scalable, human-centered advising.

items.title: From Pedagogical Mediation to Algorithmic Presence: Generative AI and the Transformation of the Educational Relationship
items.abstract: In the contemporary landscape, an epistemological and educational crisis is becoming increasingly apparent, affecting the ways in which knowledge is produced and legitimised (Quattrociocchi, 2023). Learning is gradually moving away from the notion of a slow, dialogical process based on the accumulation of experience, and is taking on the characteristics of rapid, performance-oriented acquisition (Allouche, 2024). The educational relationship is also affected by this transformation, as the links that have long ensured consistency in educational processes are becoming weaker (Lingua & Zamengo, 2025). The erosion of mediation processes diminishes recognition of their value in the construction of knowledge and the formation of the individual. The authority of teachers and experts is facing a crisis of legitimacy, whilst algorithmic systems are increasingly perceived as reliable and impartial sources of knowledge. Similar dynamics are also at play in the realm of relationships and emotions. items.title: From People Data to Decision Intelligence: Gaps in Generative Population Simulation and a Consent-First Architecture
items.abstract: Organisations make consequential decisions — product launches, pricing, policy changes — on behalf of populations they cannot observe directly. Two technologies promise to close this gap: people-data infrastructure, which indexes who individuals are, and generative population simulation, which uses large language model (LLM) agents to predict how people will respond. We argue that neither, alone or combined as currently practised, yields reliable decision intelligence. We identify seven gaps: coverage bias toward online, English-speaking, Western populations; unclear consent and provenance of grounding data; reliance on stated rather than revealed behaviour; static rather than temporal modelling; individuals simulated without social networks; the absence of decision-level evaluation standards; and a missing link between predicted reactions and the decision a firm must take. We propose a four-layer architecture — a consented, predictive people layer; a twin engine; a simulation runtime; and a decision layer — and an evaluation agenda based on back-testing against historical outcomes. We show that because decisions are comparisons, shared model bias and individual noise largely cancel, leaving option-specific cultural bias as the error that matters most. This is a position paper. It reports no new experiments; figures in Section 6 are explicitly assumed planning targets, not findings. items.title: From reflective journal to ai-mediated digital storytelling: fostering professional reflection in special education teacher training
items.abstract: In increasingly complex and technology-rich educational environments, teachers are expected not only to master instructional strategies but also to critically interpret educational situations and make pedagogically informed decisions. Professional reflection has therefore become a fundamental component of teacher education, enabling educators to connect experience with pedagogical action (Dewey, 1933; Schön, 1983; Mortari, 2003). Within this perspective, the reflective journal functions as a self-narrative pedagogical device through which teachers reinterpret classroom situations, strengthening professional judgement and inclusive educational decision-making. From a narrative perspective, reflection transforms experience into meaning (Bruner, 1992). Digital storytelling has also been recognised as an effective strategy for fostering reflection and professional learning (Robin, 2008; Banzato, 2014; De Marco & Colazzo, 2021; Mazzini et al., 2025). At the same time, recent research has highlighted both the educational potential of generative AI and the need for its pedagogically grounded integration into teacher education (Holmes et al., 2019; Tan et al., 2025). items.title: From Representation to Readout: Mechanistic Analysis of Membership Signals in Language Models
items.abstract: Membership inference aims to determine whether a particular example was included in a model's training data. Such membership signals are often broadly described as memorization, while the underlying mechanisms can involve both how information is represented internally and how it is accessed by the model to produce behaviors. We therefore present a mechanistic study of membership signals in large language models (LLMs). We introduce Decodable Information Score, Used Information Score, and Readout Accessibility Gap (DUG), a set of complementary measures that separately quantify membership information decodable from internal representations and the extent to which it is exposed through the model's readout. Across supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and reinforcement learning (RL)-based membership inference methods, membership-specific effects appear in both the amount of decodable information and readout under SFT, while under RL-based membership inference methods they appear primarily in readout. Activation patching further localizes this membership-specific effect to intermediate layers. To examine whether these findings extend to a more general RL setting, we further study reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) contamination, where the training reward is independent of the reference solution. In this setting, we find that behavioral changes can emerge without a corresponding increase in likelihood-based membership inference signals.

items.title: From Small to Large: Assessing Medical Reasoning, Benchmark Contamination, and Model Size in Language Models
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) now answer medical exam questions at or above expert level, but it is unclear whether such scores reflect clinical competence, or are instead affected by the format of the questions being asked (e.g., multiple-choice versus open-ended), prior exposure to the benchmarks, and the difficulty of the questions. These benchmarks are also public and widely used online, which may be resulting in LLM memorization. Models may perform better on questions that they have seen before. It is also not evident whether smaller models, which are more locally deployable in HIPAA-compliant hospital settings, have achieved human performance. In this study, we evaluate fourteen current models from six leading providers, one smaller and one larger model from each provider with two additional open-weight models, on 3,076 questions from four medical benchmarks (MedQA-USMLE, MedMCQA, PubMedQA, and MedBullets) under standard multiple choice, the same questions with the answer choices withheld, and reconstruction of a hidden question from its choices alone. In the standard multiple-choice setting, the strongest models exceed the human-expert baseline on MedQA-USMLE and PubMedQA, but the smaller models trail their larger models by 8.7 percentage points and only two of the six pass the human-expert bar on the licensing examination. Withholding the answer choices, however, makes every model struggle: mean accuracy falls from 82.3% to 50.9%, and the two largest drops belong to the medically specialised models. On memorization, the strongest models reconstruct one question in four from the answer choices alone, yet accuracy holds on the questions they cannot reconstruct. We further weigh accuracy against inference cost and test whether ensembling several models improves medical question answering.

items.abstract: Abstract The integration of artificial intelligence (AI) in education is rapidly reshaping learning and assessment, offering unprecedented opportunities for creativity, personalization, and efficiency. This chapter explores the complex nexus between AI, creativity, and assessment. The SAMR model (i.e., substitution, augmentation, modification, and redefinition) is applied to examine how AI is utilized across a spectrum of assessment practices, from substitution and augmentation to modification and redefinition. The findings show that although AI holds the potential to enhance creative thinking through adaptive learning and intelligent tutoring, it also elicits concerns regarding the potential for limiting originality, fostering cognitive dependency, and the mechanization of learning.

items.title: From the Zoo to the BULLPEN: Sample-Efficient LLM Profiling via Multi-Channel Model Embeddings
items.abstract: Choosing among the hundreds of thousands of available large language models (LLMs) requires a thorough understanding of each candidate model's properties. In practice, each property is measured by its own benchmark suite, so profiling a model on many properties means paying for many separate evaluations. To address this, model embeddings compress each model into a fixed-length vector from which many properties can be predicted. Existing methods, such as EmbedLLM, build these vectors from correctness patterns and question features, and often need large probe batteries to do so. However, many behaviors that are important when choosing a model, such as its verbosity, safety and style, show up more in how it answers than in whether it is correct. We introduce BULLPEN (Behavioral Understanding of Large Language models via Profile ENcodings), a framework that extends EmbedLLM in three ways. First, BULLPEN organizes the downstream tasks that prior work uses and adds 20 task benchmarks we built on behavior, style and provenance. Second, it is the first framework to read a model's own answer text jointly with its correctness and the question text. Third, it encodes models from a few hundred questions instead of the full 24,118-question pool. Across 260 open-weight models, our answer-text encoder scores 0.48 +/- 0.10 on the new tasks against 0.35 +/- 0.10 for the best prior encoder. Our encoders that read answer text keep at least 91% of their full-pool skill from only 400 questions (1.3% of the inference compute of the full question pool), while a correctness-only baseline keeps 83% with the same 400 questions. Because these embeddings need only model outputs, they support behavioral auditing and low-cost profiling, and could extend to API-only models. Code and data: https://github.com/wcquesera/bullpen

items.title: From Theory to Evaluation: Deriving the Transcultural Nurse-AI Synergy Model for Systematic Assessment of AI Outputs
items.abstract: INTRODUCTION: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly integrated into nursing education, research, and practice, raising concerns about cultural relevance, ethical integrity, and preservation of human-centered care. To address these challenges, the Transcultural Nurse-Artificial Intelligence (TCN-AI) Synergy Model was developed. METHODS: Using Walker and Avant's theory derivation method, the model was derived from the Translation Validity Index. Core concepts were identified, redefined, and extended to explain the interaction between AI-generated outputs and transcultural nursing expertise. RESULTS: The model conceptualizes this interaction as an iterative process of appraisal, contextualization, and refinement. Also, the accompanying AI Output Evaluation Rubric was developed to systematically assess AI-generated content for cultural relevance, conceptual validity, ethical integrity, and clinical relevance across nursing education, research, and practice. DISCUSSION: The TCN-AI Synergy Model advances transcultural nursing theory, education, research, and practice by providing a practical framework for critically evaluating AI-generated outputs. The accompanying rubric potentially enables efficient, systematic assessment while supporting informed decision-making in academic, research, and clinical settings.

items.title: From Transcription to Reformulation: Defining and Benchmarking Grounded Generative Speech Recognition
items.abstract: Speech language models have expanded automatic speech recognition (ASR) from transcription to general speech-to-text generation. Yet existing benchmarks still assume a single ground-truth transcript per utterance, an assumption that struggles when models produce readable, formatted, or structured outputs. In this work, we introduce Grounded Generative Speech Recognition (GSR), reformulating speech recognition as generating semantically grounded text instead of a single transcript. We define a grounded reformulation space that characterizes all valid textual realizations supported by the input speech, and establish a four-level hierarchy of reformulation capabilities, including literal transcription, canonical reformulation, semantic reformulation and speech-grounded structuring. Based on this formulation, we present GSR-Bench, the first comprehensive benchmark designed to evaluate generative speech recognition systems beyond exact transcript matching. GSR-Bench covers diverse scenarios including refined meeting transcription, cross-dialect translation, context-aware speech understanding, and robustness under silent or noisy acoustic conditions. To address the limitations of word-level evaluation metrics, we develop a multi-dimensional evaluation framework combining speech grounding assessment and LLM-based semantic judgment, whose reliability is validated through human preference studies. Extensive experiments across representative architectures, ranging from conventional ASR systems to end-to-end Speech-LLMs, reveal fundamental trade-offs between transcription fidelity and generative reformulation ability. Our analysis further identifies critical failure modes, including acoustic hallucination, unsupported generation, and instruction drift, providing insights into the design and evaluation of future grounded generative speech systems.

items.title: Frontiers: Reducing Disparity Between LLMs and Humans: Optimal LLM Sample Calibration
items.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to measure preferences and opinions, but outputs vary across prompts, personas, and model checkpoints, leaving analysts with multiple noisy elicitation variants and no principled way to combine them. Existing practice typically relies on heuristic aggregation---uniform averaging, population-weighted post-stratification, or selecting the single best subgroup---which uses fixed ex ante weights and can remain misaligned with human benchmarks. We propose Human Mimicry Calibration (HuMCal), a post-hoc calibration method that learns credibility weights over elicitation variants using only aggregate benchmark data, with no access to model internals or subgroup-level labels. HuMCal is model-agnostic and baseline-safe on the calibration split: its optimized loss weakly dominates any fixed-weight rule over the same subgroup set, including uniform weighting, post-stratification, and the best single subgroup. We evaluate HuMCal in a revealed-preference market-structure application using U.S. bank-card transactions and in a public-opinion application using Pew survey data. Across both settings, HuMCal improves alignment on the calibration split relative to all fixed-weight baselines. Out of sample, source-learned weights outperform heuristic baselines across time, geography, industry, and topic in the large majority of evaluations, although transfer is empirical rather than guaranteed. Recalibration with newer LLM checkpoints often improves alignment further. These results suggest that HuMCal can serve as a scalable calibration tool for LLM-based measurement when collecting fresh benchmark data for each target setting is costly.

items.title: Future Directions in Classroom Creativity Assessment
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter explores the potential of generative artificial intelligence (AI) to provide fit-for-purpose assessments of product creativity in a classroom context. The chapter discusses the drivers behind the need for classroom creativity assessment and focuses on the factors central to the fitness-for-purpose of creativity assessments, including quality, logistics, and authenticity. The chapter then explores these issues through a custom GPT in the OpenAI/ChatGPT large language model (LLM) environment. The custom GPT is tested (a) to explore its ability to provide meaningful summative evaluations (i.e., numerical scores) of creativity (by comparing the custom GPT scores with human evaluations of creative writing and mousetrap designs) and (b) to explore its ability to provide meaningful formative feedback (by examining its evaluation of different paper airplane designs). The chapter concludes by suggesting that generative AI (specifically LLMs) has good potential to address long-standing issues of the fitness-for-purpose of classroom creativity assessments. In the era of Industry 4, and the rise of creativity as an essential 21st-century skill, the ability to assess creativity in the classroom is the key to ensuring that students are prepared for the challenges of the future of work.

items.title: Future of work in the era of AI: how technology strategy shapes daily job roles
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to explore the impact of organizational technology strategies, particularly in the context of artificial intelligence (AI), on employees’ daily job activities. It also looks at the extent of the transformation and the role of leadership, supportive of innovation and cultural change, in reinforcing the transformation. Design/methodology/approach The researcher adopted a quantitative research design based on the survey data collected from employees in various industries in Pakistan. The researcher used structural equation modeling to analyze the relationships among technology strategies, organizational facilitators and the transformation of job roles. Findings The research shows that organizations that implement AI and automation alongside digitized processes and advanced data analysis capabilities will experience fundamental changes in their employees’ work functions, skills and job duties. The implementation of digital strategies enhances operational efficiency, but their impact extends beyond this benefit, as they completely transform how work is executed. The presence of an innovation-supportive culture together with strong leadership commitment creates an enhanced effect. The combination of encouragement of organizational experimentation and active leadership support for technological change results in more visible and positive changes in job responsibilities. Practical implications The research findings demonstrate that organizations need to combine technology investments with operational changes to achieve successful digital transformation outcomes. Organizations must establish supportive cultures together with proactive leadership to assist employees throughout the process of organizational change. Organizations need to develop their employees’ skills and build adaptable workforces while maintaining open communication to implement meaningful job role changes that last over time. Originality/value The research contributes to the future of work literature by examining how workers change their job functions at the individual-employee level rather than observing outcomes at the organizational level. The research describes how organizations use technology strategies and organizational enablers to create distinct work environments for the AI age by integrating Job Demands–Resources and Socio-Technical Systems perspectives.

items.title: GCMDiff: a condition-guided diffusion framework for pharmacophore-fragment drug discovery and target-specific molecular design
items.abstract: Drug discovery remains a costly and time-consuming process, motivating the development of artificial intelligence approaches to accelerate molecular design. Many generative models, including generative pre-trained transformers (GPT), rely on one-dimensional SMILES representations that lack explicit structural topology and are constrained by rigid syntax rules. Moreover, most existing models perform unconditional molecule generation, while the few conditional diffusion approaches often rely on abstract parameters rather than pharmacologically interpretable constraints. Consequently, current methods have limited ability to enforce explicit drug-like and pharmacophore requirements during molecular generation. Here, we propose GCMDiff, a multi-condition guided diffusion framework for molecular graph generation that supports controllable and interpretable molecular design. Unlike SMILES-based models, GCMDiff employs an atom-pair and bond-centric molecular graph representation that directly captures explicit chemical topologies. Crucially, we introduce an interpretable pharmacological condition embedding that integrates multi-modal constraints, including atom number, Lipinski’s Rule of Five constraints, and structural moieties derived from Checkmol, PubChem, and Rings in Drugs descriptors. These explicit features guide the diffusion process toward promising chemical spaces satisfying user-defined prerequisites. Benchmark experiments demonstrate that GCMDiff generates chemically valid and structurally diverse molecules, achieving 99.6% novelty and 100% uniqueness while maintaining atom and bond distributions consistent with drug-like chemical space. As a practical application, GCMDiff was applied to epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR) inhibitor design, where generated candidates reproduced key binding interactions, including the conserved hydrogen bond between a quinazoline scaffold and residue Met793. These results demonstrate that GCMDiff provides a flexible and interpretable framework for pharmacophore-fragment-conditioned molecular generation, enabling controllable exploration of drug-like chemical space and facilitating early-stage rational drug discovery. Scientific contribution GCMDiff advances molecular design by employing a graph-based diffusion framework that bypasses SMILES-related syntax limitations. Its core innovation is a multi-modal condition encoder integrating drug-like properties and pharmacophores, enabling interpretable, pharmacophore-fragment-conditioned molecular generation. The model achieves 99.6% novelty and 100% uniqueness while demonstrating practical utility through the design of novel EGFR inhibitors that replicate essential Met793 binding interactions. This framework effectively bridges generative AI with rational, constraint-driven lead optimization.

items.abstract: The article addresses the topical issue of using generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in working with academic texts by combining practical work with GenAI, the analysis of dissertation abstracts, and the development of students’ critical attitudes toward AI-generated information. This study investigates the ability of generative artificial intelligence to reconstruct selected conceptual components of academic discourse without direct access to the corresponding dissertation abstract. The study analyzes contemporary scholarly approaches to the use of generative artificial intelligence in academic discourse. The aim of the study is to empirically determine the extent to which GenAI can reproduce the relevance, research aim, and research focus of an academic study based on a minimal set of input data. The methodology involved an experimental procedure with 25 undergraduate students enrolled in the program “Language and Literature (German). Translation” within the field of Germanic languages and literatures. The empirical material comprised 25 abstracts of successfully defended dissertations on Germanic linguistics. Two generative AI systems, ChatGPT and Gemini, were used in the experiment. Following a standardized prompting procedure, the systems were provided with the research topic, but the corresponding dissertation abstract was not made available to them. The AI-generated responses were compared with the corresponding conceptual components of the dissertation abstracts using comparative content analysis. The results indicate that GenAI can semantically reconstruct selected characteristics of an existing academic study, including its relevance, research aim, and focus. At the same time, the findings do not indicate textual copying of dissertation abstracts but rather suggest the possibility of reconstructing their content-related characteristics from limited input data. These results indicate the considerable potential of GenAI as a tool for supporting academic writing. Practical implications. The findings may be used to develop university curricula that establish a balanced approach to integrating generative artificial intelligence into the educational process while preserving fundamental principles of academic integrity and values.

items.title: General-purpose foundation models surpass specialized ones on chemical property prediction tasks
items.abstract: Foundation models (FMs) learn reusable representations from large collections of unlabeled data. In chemistry the corresponding data mainly consists of molecular structures, which are abundant, whereas experimental measurements are scarce. Chemical FMs such as ChemBERTa and MoLFormer were therefore trained on diverse molecular structures to enable fine-tuning on small experimental datasets (less than 100 datapoints in most realistic scenarios) and subsequent property prediction. At the same time, general-purpose FMs such as GPT-6 Astra and Claude Opus 5.5 were trained on virtually all publicly available data, including knowledge of the humankind on molecular properties and laws governing them. Here we compare accuracies of chemical and general-purpose FMs on tasks from various areas of chemistry. Strikingly, general-purpose GPT-6 Astra outperforms the currently eligible chemical FMs on five physicochemical and quantum-chemical regression tasks when only 60 experimental datapoints are available. Only when provided 10x datapoints do the best chemical FMs reach performance of GPT-6 Astra: on 1,000 and 10,000 points they show performance on par with Astra on 60 and 1,000 points, respectively. Thus, counterintuitively, frontier general-purpose FMs are better suited for guiding chemical research in data-scarce areas than specialized chemical FMs, suggesting that learning relevant primitives (e.g. chemical structures) does not substitute training on relevant humankind knowledge.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI AND THE RESHAPING OF SECOND LANGUAGE WRITING: A COGNITIVE PROCESS PERSPECTIVE
items.abstract: Addressing how Generative AI (GenAI) reshapes the cognitive act of second language (L2) writing, this conceptual article draws on recent empirical literature (2023–2026). It grounds its analysis in the Cognitive Process Theory of Writing (CPTW), chosen because its decomposition of planning, translating, and reviewing under working-memory limits illuminates how cognitive labor is redistributed between learner and machine. Through CPTW, three key insights emerge. First, planning undergoes an externalization of productive struggle: offloading idea generation causes learners to bypass essential rhetorical problem framing. Second, translating experiences a voice constraint: model optimization toward conventionality flattens non-standard L2 syntax and homogenizes authorial voice. Third, reviewing suffers a reviewing bifurcation, splitting evaluation into goal-level appraisal and opaque decision-level monitoring. Theoretically, GenAI transforms writing into a co-generative sociotechnical practice requiring GenAI feedback literacy. Pedagogically, educators should adopt process-oriented assessments, using pre-prompting framing logs, annotated drafts, and prompt histories to evaluate cognitive engagement over polished final products.

items.title: Generative AI as a Co-Creator in Innovation Management
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is reshaping innovation management by moving beyond its conventional role as a technological tool toward becoming an active participant in creative and decision-making processes. This chapter examines how GenAI can function as a co-creator across the innovation process and explores the complementary roles of human and artificial intelligence in generating meaningful innovation outcomes. Adopting a structured integrative literature review approach, the study synthesizes recent research on GenAI-enabled innovation through thematic analysis and conceptual synthesis. The findings indicate that GenAI contributes across multiple stages of innovation, including opportunity recognition, idea generation and evaluation, product and service development, business model innovation, commercialization, and organizational innovation. Its primary strengths lie in rapid content generation, knowledge synthesis, recombination, scenario development, and iterative refinement, whereas human contributors remain central to problem framing, contextual interpretation, strategic and ethical judgment, validation, and accountability. Building on these complementary capabilities, the chapter proposes the Human–GenAI Innovation Co-Creation Framework, which conceptualizes innovation as an iterative cycle of framing, generating, evaluating, refining, validating, and experimenting. The analysis further identifies hallucination, bias and idea homogenization, intellectual property concerns, human over-reliance, AI literacy, and organizational governance as important boundary conditions shaping the effectiveness of co-creation. Overall, the chapter argues that the transformative potential of GenAI in innovation management lies not in replacing human innovators but in designing organizational processes that deliberately combine human judgment and creativity with GenAI’s generative and synthetic capabilities.

items.title: Generative AI as Metacognitive Scaffolding in Undergraduate Mathematics: A Quasi-Experimental Study of Problem-Solving Performance and Engagement
items.abstract: Abstract This study examines whether generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can improve university students’ mathematical problem-solving when it is designed not as an answer generator but as a metacognitive scaffold. Building on sociocultural scaffolding, self-regulated learning, and Pólya’s problem-solving model, the study tested a 15-week structured GenAI-supported intervention in Calculus I. A cluster-assigned quasi-experimental pre-test/post-test design was implemented with 128 undergraduates distributed across four tutorial sections: two sections used a Socratic GenAI protocol (n = 60), and two sections received traditional instruction using the same weekly problem sets (n = 68). Students’ solutions were scored with a validated analytic rubric aligned with the four Pólya stages, and outcomes were analyzed using ANCOVA with pre-test adjustment and a multilevel sensitivity model for section-level clustering. Results showed a statistically significant adjusted between-group difference favoring the GenAI-supported group, F(1, 125) = 28.76, p < .001, partial eta squared = .187, with the largest stage-specific effects for carrying out the plan and understanding the problem. Student perceptions were highly positive, and cognitive engagement showed the strongest association with performance gains. The study contributes to educational psychology by specifying a testable instructional mechanism: structured GenAI-supported instruction may support mathematical problem solving when prompts elicit planning, monitoring, explanation, and reflection while discouraging direct solution-seeking.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence and Creativity in Kindergarten Through Grade 12 Education
items.abstract: Abstract The rapid rise of generative AI (GenAI) presents both opportunities and challenges for fostering creativity in kindergarten through Grade 12 (K–12) education. This systematic scoping review analyzes 45 studies (2017–2025) to examine how GenAI is applied in creative learning. The chapter identifies four main categories: creativity assessment, human–AI co-creativity, stakeholders’ perceptions, and creativity enhancement. Findings reveal a dominant focus on language-based tasks such as storytelling, with limited attention to auditory, embodied, or spatial creativity. Although GenAI tools show potential in supporting idea generation, multimodal expression, and co-creation, most studies lack theoretical grounding and comprehensive assessment methods. Frameworks such as the 4C model or evidence-centered design are rarely used, and equity concerns—such as access, cultural representation, and student agency—remain underexplored. Although emerging GenAI tools enable personalized feedback and formative assessment, they also raise questions about authorship transparency and ethical use. This chapter provides a foundation for advancing equitable and responsible integration of GenAI to support creativity in K–12 education. It advocates for ethically grounded, theory-informed, and developmentally appropriate GenAI designs that enhance rather than automate creativity.

items.title: Generative artificial intelligence and terminology work: structural associations of prompt strategy preference, cognitive load, and self-efficacy
items.abstract: Introduction The widespread application of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in knowledge-intensive domains requires continuous adjustment of human cognitive patterns. In terminology work, aligning strict semantic standards against the non-deterministic output of large language models (LLMs) is closely intertwined with workers' subjective cognitive load. This study examines the structural associations among prompt strategy preference, AI interaction self-efficacy, and subjective cognitive load, while testing the potential moderating role of professional experience. Methods Based on cross-sectional survey data from 1,760 practitioners using LLMs for terminology tasks, structural equation modeling (SEM) and latent profile analysis (LPA) were employed. SEM evaluated the linear structural associations among prompt strategy preference, self-efficacy, and cognitive load, while LPA identified behavioral user profiles. Multi-group equivalence testing was further conducted across three career stages (novices, intermediates, and experts). Results Prompt strategy preference is significantly and negatively associated with subjective cognitive load, with AI interaction self-efficacy serving as a significant mediator in this structural relationship. LPA identified three distinct user profiles (low, medium, and high strategy use), with the high strategy group exhibiting the lowest cognitive load and highest self-efficacy. Multi-group equivalence tests indicated no statistically significant moderation across experience cohorts, demonstrating structural invariance of the core model across career stages. Discussion From the perspective of cognitive ergonomics, upfront prompt structuring is structurally linked to downstream cognitive offloading and psychological buffering. These findings provide empirical evidence for individual cognitive resilience during human-AI collaboration in the generative AI era.

items.title: GeoPROV: A Semantic Provenance Profile for Coastal EO-Derived Products Informed by a Systematic Review of Spatial Data Supply Chains
items.abstract: Emerging remote sensing technologies increasingly support coastal observation through Earth observation (EO) derivatives such as satellite-derived shorelines, unmanned aerial vehicle (UAV)- and light detection and ranging (LiDAR)-based elevation models, coastal land-use/land-cover products, bathymetric grids, turbidity and chlorophyll-a indicators, habitat maps, flood extents, and artificial intelligence (AI)-generated segmentation outputs. These EO-derived products are central to shoreline monitoring, coastal vulnerability assessment, flood-response planning, marine ecosystem management, and land–sea administration. Yet their evidential value depends on transparent provenance: users must know which sensor, acquisition condition, preprocessing chain, algorithm, model version, validation dataset, and uncertainty estimate produced each coastal product. The review synthesises 156 eligible publications identified through a systematic review process. Of these, 89 studies containing sufficient implementation and methodological detail were selected for detailed analytical coding. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) protocol, the review analyses application domains, provenance capture modes, representation strategies, semantic web technologies, and interoperability practices. A coastal EO thematic refinement translates the review findings into provenance requirements for satellite, UAV, LiDAR, Internet of Things (IoT), open-water, and AI-enabled coastal observation workflows. The review identifies persistent gaps in feature-level lineage, alignment between the World Wide Web Consortium Provenance Ontology (PROV-O) and International Organization for Standardization (ISO) geospatial metadata standards, spatial semantics, AI workflow transparency, uncertainty traceability, and scalable querying. To address these limitations, the paper introduces GeoPROV, a lightweight semantic profile of PROV-O designed for spatially explicit, feature-level provenance. GeoPROV aligns PROV-O with ISO 19115/19157, GeoSPARQL, Shapes Constraint Language (SHACL), and SpatioTemporal Asset Catalogue (STAC)-compatible catalogue practices. The framework enables EO-derived coastal products to be traced from raw observation through preprocessing, AI/geoprocessing, validation, catalogue publication, and coastal-administrative decision-making. The resulting GeoPROV profile integrates PROV-O, GeoSPARQL, SHACL, ISO 19115/19157 lineage concepts, and STAC metadata within a lightweight semantic framework demonstrated through a coastal EO product workflow and machine-actionable provenance implementation.

items.title: Global Burden, Temporal Trends, and Risk Factors of Low Back Pain Among People Aged 15–49 Years
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Low back pain (LBP) remains a leading cause of disability worldwide. However, the disease burden among people aged 15-49 years has been insufficiently addressed. OBJECTIVE: The present study aimed to investigate the global burden, temporal trends, and attributable risk factors of low back pain among people aged 15-49 years. METHODS: Using data from the Global Burden of Disease (GBD) study 2021, we analyzed the incidence, prevalence, and disability-adjusted life years (DALYs) of LBP across 204 countries and territories. Age-standardized rates (ASRs) were calculated, and temporal trends from 1990 to 2021 were examined using joinpoint regression. RESULTS: According to GBD 2021 estimates, there are approximately 16,993,809 new cases of LBP that occurred worldwide, with South Asia bearing the highest case load. Although ASRs of incidence (AAPC: -0.16; 95% CI: -0.20, -0.12), ASRs of prevalence (AAPC: -0.17; 95% CI: -0.20, -0.14), and ASRs of DALYs (AAPC: -0.16; 95% CI: -0.18, -0.14) declined between 1990 and 2021, absolute case numbers and DALYs increased. Occupational ergonomic factors (28.4%, 95% CI: 26.3%-30.7%), tobacco smoking (11.4%, 95% CI: 7.6%-15.2%), and high body mass index (BMI) (10.9%, 95% CI: 1.1%-21.0%) were the major attributable risk factors. Women always bear a more severe disease burden than men, with the age-standardized incidence rate (ASIR) being 3788.64 vs. 2380.94 per 100,000; the age-standardized prevalence rate (ASPR) being 8822.52 vs. 5410.51 per 100,000; and the age-standardized DALY rates (ASDR) being 999.13 vs. 626.28 per 100,000 in women and men, respectively. When it comes to the socio-demographic index (SDI), ASIR and ASPR initially increased with rising SDI, reaching a peak in Australasia, with ASPR over 12,500 per 100,000 and ASIR over 5000 per 100,000, before subsequently decreasing with further SDI increments. CONCLUSIONS: Despite declining ASRs, the absolute global burden of LBP among individuals aged 15-49 continues to grow, particularly among women and in high-SDI regions. Targeted preventive strategies and control measures are urgently needed.

items.title: Governing AI-Assisted Board Decisions: A Dual-Lock Model for Information Independence and Accountability
items.abstract: Purpose: This study develops a governance architecture for board-governed strategic decisions in which artificial intelligence (AI) provides common advice while legal and organizational decision ownership remains human. It examines two linked risks: erosion of independent human information and distortion of delegation through outcome-dependent credit and blame. Methodology/Approach: A theoretical decision-economic model is used to formalize firm-optimal and executive-optimal delegation, an endogenous attribution wedge, common-AI-induced error covariance, and boundary conditions for pre-AI information recording. The analysis treats governance controls as ex-ante commitments rather than ex-post corrections. Findings: Common exposure to an imperfect AI signal can increase correlation among revised human judgments and reduce the effective number of independent checks. Separately, private attribution incentives can move delegation away from the firm-optimal benchmark. The proposed Information Lock records designated human assessments before common AI exposure, while the Accountability Lock fixes effective decision rights and attribution rules before outcomes are known. The model also identifies limits: perfectly reconstructible post-AI judgments reduce the Information Lock mainly to an auditability device, while residual career downside can shift distortion from over-delegation toward rejection or delay of positive-value decisions. Conclusion: The contribution is a unified, selective governance architecture linking information independence and outcome-invariant accountability. It provides boards and senior executives with an implementable framework for preserving informational diversity, clarifying decision ownership, and distinguishing poor process from unfavorable stochastic outcomes in AI-assisted strategic decisions.

items.title: Harnessing artificial intelligence for academic development: a bibliometric analysis of personalized learning, adaptive feedback, and collaborative growth
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly discussed as a catalyst for transforming academic development by enabling more personalized, responsive, and collaborative professional learning. However, the research landscape remains fragmented across diverse themes and methodological approaches. This study provides a bibliometric and thematic synthesis of AI-related research relevant to academic development, focusing on personalized learning, adaptive feedback, and collaborative growth. Using a systematic review protocol informed by PRISMA and PICO frameworks, 507 peer-reviewed studies published between 2020 and 2024 were identified from major academic databases. Bibliometric analysis examined publication trends, thematic clusters, and methodological patterns, followed by a qualitative synthesis of findings related to academic development outcomes. The results indicate three dominant directions. First, AI-driven personalization is widely reported as supporting tailored learning pathways and just-in-time instructional support. Second, adaptive feedback systems, including intelligent tutoring systems and automated analytics tools, are associated with improvements in instructional decision-making and pedagogical reflection. Third, AI-supported collaborative environments are emerging as mechanisms for peer learning, mentorship, and knowledge exchange. Adoption remains uneven, with barriers including ethical concerns, digital readiness, and varying faculty acceptance. Overall, AI technologies hold significant potential to enhance academic development when integrated with institutional support, ethical governance, and context-sensitive implementation strategies.

items.title: Hopelessness among Healthcare Workers during the COVID-19 Pandemic: Experiences and Perceptions
items.abstract: Background: COVID-19 has globally challenged health systems and created profound psychosocial consequences for healthcare workers. Hopelessness, as a negative future expectation, may emerge alongside fear, anxiety, and burnout. This study aimed to examine hopelessness levels among healthcare workers during the COVID-19 pandemic and to identify associated factors based on their experiences and perceptions.Methods: The research group consisted of all employees at an education and research hospital. Data were collected from 562 personnel (48.2% of active staff). The data collection tools included a questionnaire and the Beck Hopelessness Scale. Statistical analyses included descriptive statistics, independent samples t-test, one-way ANOVA with Bonferroni/Tamhane post-hoc tests, and stepwise multiple linear regression model.Results: The mean age was 35.8±8.8 years, and the mean length of service was 9.1±8.3 years. Of the participants, 61.2% were female, 30.8% were doctors, and 27.0% nurses. Nearly one-third had worked in COVID-19 units, one-third had been infected, and more than half had directly cared for COVID-19 patients. In bivariate analyses, smoking, workplace reassignment, direct care of patients with COVID-19, and perceiving colleagues’ knowledge as insufficient were associated with higher hopelessness. In the multivariable model, female gender, chronic illness or disability, a mixed work schedule, psychological impact, the belief that the pandemic could not be controlled, and pessimistic expectations about returning to normal life remained independently associated with hopelessness.Conclusion: Hopelessness is a critical psychological concern among healthcare workers in pandemic disasters. Early recognition of vulnerable groups and institutional support to reduce uncertainty, provide adequate Personal Protective Equipment, and regulate shift work are essential to strengthen workforce resilience. These findings highlight the need to integrate psychological well-being into pandemic preparedness and occupational health policies.

items.title: How Artificial Intelligence Facilitates Sustainable Food Consumption: The Mediating Roles of Perceived Usefulness and Trust
items.abstract: Background As climate concerns intensify and artificial intelligence transforms retail experiences, understanding how AI tools influence sustainable consumption decisions has become increasingly critical. This study investigates how AI-assisted shopping affects consumer purchase intentions for plant-based proteins—a key lever for dietary sustainability—by examining the mediating roles of perceived usefulness and trust in AI technology. Drawing on the Technology Acceptance Model, we propose that AI usage and environmental concern influence purchase intentions through dual cognitive and affective pathways. Method We test this framework using survey data from 519 Amazon customers in the United States, analyzed through Partial Least Squares Structural Equation Modeling with 5,000 bootstrap resamples. The measurement model demonstrates excellent psychometric properties, with all constructs exceeding recommended thresholds for reliability and validity. Results The study reveals that both AI usage and environmental concern significantly enhance perceived usefulness of AI for sustainability decisions and trust in AI recommendations, which subsequently drive plant-based protein purchase intentions. The effects operate entirely through these mediating mechanisms, with perceived usefulness showing stronger influence than trust. The model explains 22.4% of variance in purchase intentions, indicating substantial explanatory power for behavioral research. items.abstract: Physical inactivity and sedentary behaviour represent one of the most pressing global health challenges of the twenty-first century. Insufficient physical activity is causally associated with noncommunicable diseases, mental health disorders, and premature mortality (Bull et al., 2020; WHO, 2022). Artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising avenue for promoting physical activity at scale: AI-powered tools can deliver personalised coaching, adaptive training plans, real-time feedback, and behavioural nudges in ways that traditional interventions cannot replicate (Guerriero et al., 2026). However, the landscape of AI tools for physical activity is highly heterogeneous and research remains fragmented, with no comprehensive functional mapping of tools available to end users. This chapter addresses that gap. This contribution draws on an exploratory mapping study in which AI tools for physical activity promotion were identified through systematic navigation of There's an AI for That a directory indexing over 50,000 AI tools. items.title: How audiences navigate the tension between influencer professionalisation and authenticity: an exploration from the context of Multi-Channel Network disclosure
items.abstract: The growing professionalisation of influencers has intensified tensions surrounding authenticity, yet little is known about how audiences perceive and respond to it. This study examines how audiences interpret professionalisation through organisational cues and navigate the authenticity tensions these cues evoke, taking the Multi-Channel Network disclosure on Chinese social media as an empirical case. Based on 20 in-depth interviews, findings show that audiences interpret the disclosure as a symbol of professionalisation, which implies technical expertise and corporatised operation. Using a multidimensional authenticity framework, professionalisation is perceived to diminish influencers’ intrinsic motivation and honesty. However, rather than rejecting professionalised influencers, audiences negotiate authenticity loss by normalising professionalisation, setting boundaries of acceptance, and prioritising content usefulness and entertainment. These negotiation practices enable audiences to reconcile tensions between professionalisation and authenticity and sustain engagement with professionalised influencers.

items.title: How do Large Language Models (LLMs) Challenge Linguistics?
items.abstract: Geoffrey Hinton — often called the "Godfather of Artificial Intelligence" — has openly criticized Noam Chomsky, raising profound questions about the relationship between linguistics and artificial intelligence. This paper examines four dimensions along which large language models challenge established linguistic paradigms. First, should linguistics pursue a macro or micro-orientation? This debate concerns both the scope of linguistic inquiry and the transformation of its research methods; the paper argues that linguistics must shift from a narrow, discipline-confined perspective toward a comprehensive, interdisciplinary "macro-linguistics" that integrates with the humanities, natural sciences, medicine, and engineering, and that spans phonetics, grammar, semantics, and pragmatics. Second, are language and thought separable or inseparable? Contrary to the traditional dichotomy, this paper argues that human thought cannot be entirely separated from language: the primary purpose of thought is communication, and without new information, thought loses its vitality — artificial attempts to disconnect thought from communication are therefore counterproductive. Third, is language acquisition innate or experiential? Artificial intelligence has significantly challenged Chomsky's innateness hypothesis, abandoning the premise that language is a pre-programmed, innate ability in favor of treating language as fundamentally experiential — a shift validated by the landmark successes of experience-based learning models. Fourth, can AI possess thought, or even constitute life? The paper argues that artificial intelligence cannot possess life in the biological sense: AI's language is fundamentally disconnected from genuine thought, linguistic fluency does not equate to autonomous thinking, and AI remains an incomplete imitation of human language and cognition rather than an autonomous thinking entity.

items.title: How Much Can Tool Calls Reveal About You? Privacy Leakage from Tool-Call Traces
items.abstract: Large language model (LLM)-based agents interact with external tools through protocols such as the Model Context Protocol (MCP), producing tool-call traces that may expose behavioral signals about users. In this work, we systematically study the risk of user-profile inference from MCP tool-call traces, where observers infer user attributes from protocol-valid tool interactions without access to user conversations. We introduce PrivacyTrace, a benchmark containing 1,000 synthetic user profiles and 4,000 agent trajectories across four domains, generated with real MCP tools from 25 servers. Experiments with four mainstream LLM attackers show that tool-call traces enable a 26.25% attack success rate for profile inference, compared with 17.97% from prior-based guessing. Further analysis reveals that tool arguments and returned results provide the main trace-grounded evidence, while linking traces across sessions further amplifies profiling risk. These findings demonstrate that MCP tool-call traces can act as effective behavioral side channels for user profiling, motivating the development of privacy-aware mechanisms for agent-tool interactions. Code and data are available at https://github.com/AI45Lab/PrivacyTrace.

items.title: How university social responsibility shapes staff citizenship behavior: a theory synthesis for teaching, research, and student support
items.abstract: Universities depend on staff contributions that exceed formal duties, such as sharing teaching practices, supporting students beyond scheduled hours, and volunteering for curriculum and quality-assurance work, to sustain teaching, research, and student support. University social responsibility (USR) is enacted largely through these same staff. Yet it remains unclear when staff perceptions of USR strengthen such discretionary contributions and when they are experienced as additional, unrecognized demands. This theory-synthesis article integrates USR, micro-level corporate social responsibility, organizational behavior, and recent higher education research to explain how perceived USR may translate into organizational citizenship behavior (OCB) among academic and administrative staff. Two pathways are proposed. A relational pathway links perceived USR to organizational justice, grounded in workload allocation, teaching assignments, promotion, and participation in decisions, and then to organizational trust, work engagement, and OCB. A motivational pathway links perceived USR to intrinsic motivation, engagement, and OCB when responsibility-related academic activities support autonomy and competence. Perceived organizational support is proposed to strengthen the relationship between perceived USR and organizational trust. Eight numbered propositions (P1-P8) are developed; Proposition 7 contains two constituent serial pathways (P7a and P7b). OCB is differentiated by its target: colleagues, students, and the institution. The framework identifies professional autonomy, collegial norms, role type, and workload systems as conditions that shape these relationships. Implications concern aligning USR commitments with fair academic workload, supportive practices, and recognized voluntary collaboration that benefits teaching and the learning environment.

items.title: Human Agency and Creativity in Artificial Intelligence–Assisted Learning Environments
items.abstract: Abstract This chapter examines human creativity in artificial intelligence (AI)–assisted learning through the lens of student agency. It first reviews four theoretical perspectives on agency—instrumental, effortful, dynamically emergent, and authorial—and analyzes how each perspective frames the relationship between learner agency and creativity. Building on this synthesis, the chapter discusses how generative AI (GenAI) reshapes students’ cognitive, social, and creative participation by extending their capabilities; redistributing agency across human–AI interactions; and raising new questions about authorship, responsibility, and ethical engagement. The chapter then introduces the framework of agentic engagement with AI, which conceptualizes learner agency as a proactive, adaptable, and reciprocal process enacted through the ongoing negotiation between human intentionality and machine adaptivity. This framework is further linked to mini-c creativity, highlighting how students use GenAI to construct personally meaningful ideas, interpretations, and creative expressions. Together, these perspectives shift attention from creativity as a product or performance outcome to a process of agentic meaning-making. The chapter concludes by proposing future research directions on the processes and outcomes of creativity in AI-assisted learning.

items.title: Human Centered AI Ethics, Algorithmic Bias, and Data Synthesis in Social Work and Military Settings
items.abstract: Purpose: This study examines the ethical and professional implications of integrating Artificial Intelligence (AI) into clinical and community Social Work and its application within military settings, focusing on algorithmic bias, AI assisted data synthesis, privacy, and the preservation of human judgment. Research Methodology: The study adopts a qualitative documentary research design that draws on peer reviewed literature, professional standards, international policy documents, and relevant national frameworks. The documents were analyzed thematically through the lenses of Human Centered Design Theory, Sociotechnical Systems Theory, and the Social Justice Perspective. Results: AI offers opportunities to improve assessment, documentation, psychosocial intervention, research, and organizational decision making, but it raises serious concerns about privacy, confidentiality, informed consent, accountability, algorithmic bias, and transparency. These concerns intensify in military settings, where AI systems may process highly sensitive personal, health, and operational information about personnel, veterans, and their families. Conclusions: AI should be treated as a professional support technology rather than a substitute for Social Work judgment, therapeutic relationships, or accountable institutional decision making. Responsible adoption requires institutional safeguards, professional competencies, continuous auditing, meaningful human oversight, and mechanisms through which affected people can challenge AI supported decisions. Limitations: The study relies on secondary documents, does not test specific AI systems empirically, and focuses mainly on the Nigerian policy context. Contributions: The study proposes a Human Centered AI Framework for Social Work and Military Practice (HCAI SWMP) built on ethical governance, bias aware data management, secure data synthesis, and human centered implementation.

items.abstract: Abstract A conceptual framework for understanding the intersection of human creativity and generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in education is presented in this chapter. The creative GenAI confluence framework offers a holistic perspective, serving as a lens to examine both how GenAI is used in educational contexts and its impact on human creativity and learning. Rather than viewing human creative processes and GenAI tools as merely additive, the framework conceptualizes their relationship as a complex, dynamic, and often reciprocal process, in which human and AI contributions are deeply intertwined and difficult to disentangle. This framework may support understanding common patterns of GenAI use in education and inform future research and practice across kindergarten through grade 12 and higher education settings.

items.abstract: Abstract Abstract: This chapter examines the dual role of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in augmenting and challenging human creativity, particularly within higher education contexts. Through a synthesis of contemporary literature, it explores how AI democratizes creative expression by providing advanced tools to a broad audience while also addressing concerns over overreliance, equitable access, authorship, and cognitive development. The discussion focuses on how AI-driven workflows can support divergent thinking and bolster students’ creative confidence, with structured co-creation processes that enhance rather than replace human agency. Practical challenges—such as technical infrastructure, educator preparedness, and the adaptation of assessment practices for AI-assisted work—are also reviewed. By offering a comprehensive overview of AI’s evolving influence on creativity, the chapter highlights future opportunities and ethical and cultural considerations, ultimately providing insights for researchers, educators, and policymakers seeking to navigate the shifting intersection of AI, creativity, and education.

items.title: Human likeness is a misplaced benchmark for artificial intelligence
items.abstract: Recent claims that large language models pass the Turing test span different procedures, but share a common focus on human outputs, rather than the processes that lead to those outputs. Here we challenge the inference from successful imitation to intelligence. Similar outputs can arise from different processes and conceal differences in reasoning, generalization, and adaptation. More fundamentally, we question whether human likeness should guide AI development at all. Prioritizing imitation can reproduce human biases, facilitate manipulation, and favor replacing people over augmenting their capabilities. AI systems should expand human welfare, not merely impersonate us. We recommend three coordinated changes: designing systems that strengthen human capabilities and independent judgment; requiring funded projects to assess benefits, costs, and their distribution; and guiding institutional procurement and renewal by evidence of AI’s effects on human welfare.

items.title: Human or Machine? EFL Students’ Trust Calibration in AI-Generated English Content:A Study at the Faculty of Languages, Surman
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is increasingly used by university EFL students for language learning and academic tasks, yet fluent output may be inaccurate. This study examined self-reported trust and verification practices and students’ judgments of selected AI-generated English content among undergraduates at the Faculty of Languages, Surman, University of Sabratha. A quantitative descriptive-correlational design was applied to questionnaire responses from 38 students. The instrument included background questions, ten five-point Likert items, five evaluation tasks with confidence and verification-intention responses, and an optional open-ended item. Descriptive statistics, Cronbach’s alpha, and Spearman’s rank correlations were used. Mean self-reported trust was 3.36/5 and verification was 3.74/5. Students correctly judged 62.1% of task responses under the primary answer key. Use frequency was not significantly associated with trust (ρ = .279, p = .090), whereas verification was associated with accuracy (ρ = .473, p = .003), as was confidence (ρ = .648, p < .001). Findings are preliminary given the small sample, modest trust-scale internal consistency, and ambiguity in one evaluation item. In exploratory HC3 regression, confidence remained associated with accuracy (β = .51, p = .005), while reported verification did not uniquely reach p < .05 after confidence was included (p = .063). After Holm correction across 28 exploratory pairs, only confidence–accuracy and awareness–adaptive-trust correlations remained significant. The study highlights the value of teaching verification and interpreting trust relative to output reliability.

items.title: Human-in-the-loop Artificial Intelligence for Socio-Emotional Learning in Autism: A Pedagogical Framework for Guided Interaction and Educational Responsibility
items.abstract: The progressive integration of artificial intelligence into educational contexts is reshaping approaches to instructional mediation, the personalisation of learning pathways, and interaction with students. These potential applications are particularly relevant within the field of social and emotional learning (Goleman, 2011), especially for children with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), for whom structured and predictable learning environments characterised by gradual progression may foster the development of emotional and relational competencies. However, the use of generative artificial intelligence systems requires careful consideration of the implications associated with content reliability, process transparency, and the attribution of educational responsibility (Floridi, 2022). Indeed, the fluency and apparent plausibility of AI-generated responses do not guarantee their accuracy. Human supervision and validation processes are therefore essential to ensure that the content produced is scientifically grounded, pedagogically appropriate, and consistent with the intended learning objectives. items.title: Human-in-the-Loop Pedagogy: Reframing Technical Communication Education in the Age of AI
items.abstract: Generative AI is becoming part of technical communication workflows, but programs still need a grounded way to teach students how to use it while preserving rhetorical judgment, editorial responsibility, and audience awareness. This article proposes a human-in-the-loop pedagogy that treats AI as a system whose outputs must be defined, guided, evaluated, and constrained by human writers. It offers a heuristic for integrating AI into writing instruction while reinforcing the field’s core competencies.
