items.title: Human-led, AI-enabled: preventing another AI winter through workforce transformation
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) has played a role in life sciences research and healthcare delivery for decades, though its nature and applications have changed with each new technology. As early as the 1950s, symbolic logic models provided clinical decision support: a form of deterministic AI encoded human knowledge as rules that an AI logic model could follow and implement (Nawaz et al., 2025). These early rule-based systems highlighted both the promise and limitations of symbolic AI. Subsequent periods of over-expectation followed by underdelivery contributed to recurring "AI winters" in which investment and enthusiasm declined.After 2010, computational and algorithmic developments led to machine learning (ML) and deep learning models. While these performed extremely well in some use cases (Habehh and Gohel, 2021), notably in biomedical research and image analysis, their use remained largely concentrated among technical experts and specialized applications. In the 2020s, large language models (LLMs) have rapidly changed the AI landscape in life sciences and medicine, and we are on the cusp of even faster evolutions, with state space models and active inference-based concepts that could lead to non-linear, novel leaps.The adoption of LLMs has been unlike that of any other modern technology. Most innovations, such as cars, mobile phones, and the internet, have taken years (between 1 year and 75 years) to reach adoption by 50 million users globally (Desjardins, 2018), whereas ChatGPT took only 5 days to achieve this. This unprecedented uptake leads to a paradigm shift in how we think about the users, use cases, and impact of a new technology. LLMs could change working practices in nearly every industry, to varying degrees. In their lead article, Guni et al. articulate the potential influence of LLMs in life sciences research and healthcare delivery (Guni et al. 2026). They review the rise and fall of AI applications in biomedical research and clinical decision support, and robustly discuss the elements needed for the current wave of AI to succeed. Specifically, they comment that "multidisciplinary effort (is needed) across several key domains: i) algorithmic science and architectures, ii) datasets, iii) processing power and efficiency, iv) infrastructure, v) human factors through codesign, and vi) interoperability with both legacy and modern healthcare systems." These efforts will require collaboration between clinicians, researchers, technologists, patients, ethicists, policymakers and others, and Guni et al. discuss a thorough breadth and depth of key topics. However, a seventh critical domain underlies all the others: the transformation of biomedical education and workforce development. Without a workforce capable of effectively leading AI systems, even the most sophisticated algorithms, datasets, and infrastructure will fail to deliver lasting impact, and we risk another AI winter.With respect to education, the widespread yet heterogenous use of LLMs by students and professors alike is challenging current pedagogy and assessment frameworks. In some cases, students are using LLMs to study or complete homework assignments, yet their professors lack expertise and are unprepared to alter their syllabus, homework, or exams (Lelescu et al 2025). In other cases, faculty are trying to integrate LLMs but are being met by significant resistance by students (Farinosi and Melchior, 2025). LLMs are also changing the day-to-day activities of our workforce, where adoption is similarly mixed and there is limited infrastructure to support broad, comprehensive workforce development. Many proposed educational responses focus primarily on the development of AI competencies across the continuum of learners and professionals. However, an exclusive focus on AI competencies introduces two related risks: "cognitive de-skilling", in which professionals gradually lose critical expertise and skills due to over-reliance on AI and "never-skilling", where the next generation of learners never fully develops foundational competencies because AI systems perform those tasks from the outset.Currently, health systems plan to measure the immediate augmented performance of AI tools in terms of clinical outcomes or immediate workflow efficiencies; we have yet to comprehensively measure their impact on retained competency or the longer-term implications of their use as a performance standard. Over the next 50 years, AI will likely become a critical part of many decision-making processes, training programs, and assessments done in clinical settings. However, if we never measure the retained competency of clinical staff to understand the impact of AI on long-term skill erosion, we could unintentionally introduce a critical system failure in the future. Clinicians who can no longer spot errors in AI tools or perform tasks when tools fail may put patients at risk and create a new type of AI winter-a systemic failure due to over-reliance on AI and lack of human competency. This AI winter would be extremely damaging to the practice of medicine in multiple ways: 1) direct risk to patients, 2) time to re-skill a generation of medical practitioners, and 3) lack of medical leaders with expertise to train the clinicians.Life sciences and healthcare are not the first knowledge-intensive domains to confront the challenge of maintaining human expertise as automation becomes increasingly capable. As commercial aviation systems evolved to automate key functions such as takeoff, landing, and navigation, concerns emerged that pilots were becoming overly reliant on automation, potentially eroding critical manual flying skills and reducing resilience when automated systems failed. Recognizing this risk, the United States Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) issued a Safety Alert in 2017 (FAA, 2017) and further guidance in 2022 (FAA, 2022) to strengthen policies and training that preserved pilot proficiency in manual operations.This experience provides a compelling parallel to the adoption of AI-driven clinical decision support systems. In both aviation and healthcare, humans and technology function as components of a sociotechnical system (Trist, 1981), where safety depends on the effective interaction between people, processes, and tools. When technological capabilities advance without corresponding attention to human competencies, organizations risk losing the very redundancies that protect against failure. The FAA's approach demonstrates that successful integration of automation requires more than technical performance; it requires deliberate governance, training, monitoring, and ongoing investment in human expertise. Ultimately, the safety of any automated system depends not only on the technology itself, but also on how human competency is preserved and strengthened alongside it (Macnamara et al., 2024).In short, humans must be the redundancy when technology systems fail.To avoid creating a generation of professionals who cannot function effectively when AI systems are unavailable, unreliable, or incorrect, we need radical transformation in our education and workforce development frameworks to teach both AI competencies and domain-specific competencies in synchrony. We must develop these competency frameworks now to prepare the future workforce to thrive in an AI-enabled world.Perhaps the easier competency framework is that of AI competencies. For example, prompt engineering, AI literacy, validation and oversight, ethical and responsible use of AI, agentic AI, and the nature of human-AI collaborations are obvious topics that biomedical education for life sciences research and healthcare delivery must begin to learn. Many programs around the globe have begun offering didactic and practical-based educational programs to serve this need. Perhaps more challenging is the listing of domain-specific competencies. Not every fact that previous generations were expected to memorize will remain equally valuable in an AI-enabled environment. The challenge lies in determining which foundational knowledge remains essential for independent critical thinking and reasoning, and which tasks can appropriately be augmented by AI. Future domain-specific competency frameworks may place less emphasis on memorization and greater emphasis on reasoning, interpretation, critical evaluation, communication, judgement, and collaboration. Each domain needs to develop their list of domain-specific competencies and then design pedagogy, training, and learning assessment around these competencies, assuming that AI will be a partner for the learner. Neither AI competencies nor domain-specific competencies alone are sufficient; future professionals will require mastery of both.The goal should be to leverage AI to improve the efficiency and effectiveness of biomedical research and clinical practice, allowing humans to focus on uniquely human activities such as critical thinking, creativity, and interpersonal connection, rather than repetitive and mundane tasks.Our society has seen workforce transitions before, for example as result of the invention of electricity, the Industrial Revolution, and the emergence of the internet. For example, online streaming services have rendered many jobs unnecessary, such as cashiers in video rental or record stores, while creating thousands of jobs never imagined in the 1990s. Similarly, if the current AI era succeeds some workforce roles will vanish, but many new roles will emerge, some unimaginable today. Leaders, researchers, educators, and workforce members must proactively develop systems and frameworks that enable current and future generations to thrive with AI technology at their fingertips.The future of biomedical research and healthcare should not be defined by "humans in the loop", but by "humans in the lead". Our challenge is not simply to build more capable AI systems. It is to build educational and workforce development frameworks that preserve human expertise while enabling effective human-AI partnership, i.e., systems that are "human-led, AI-enabled." History suggests that AI winters occur when technological capabilities outpace the ability of institutions, professionals, and society to effectively adopt and sustain them. Workforce transformation may therefore be one of the most important safeguards against another cycle of overpromising and underdelivering. If we succeed, AI can become one of the most transformative technologies in the history of medicine. If we fail, another AI winter may be closer than we think.

items.title: Human, AI-generated, and hybrid corrective feedback in L2 argumentative writing
items.abstract: This quasi-experimental study investigated the differential effects of human teacher feedback (HTF), AI-generated feedback (AIGF), and hybrid feedback (HF) on learner engagement and argumentative writing quality among 120 undergraduate ESL students across an eight-week intervention. Engagement (behavioural, cognitive, emotional) was measured via a purpose-built questionnaire and revision-tracking logs; writing quality was scored on a five-dimension analytic rubric. Repeated-measures ANOVA and multiple regression showed that HF was associated with the greatest improvement in writing quality (η²p = .24), HTF with the highest proportion of higher-order revisions, and AIGF with the highest revision frequency. Hybrid feedback condition membership was the strongest predictor of writing-quality improvement, followed by cognitive engagement. These findings have implications for AI-integrated writing instruction in higher education.

items.title: Hybrid HCAI - A Thought Experiment on the Ultimate Symbiosis of Human and Artificial Intelligence A Positive Future Scenario for Artificial Intelligence in Business and Society
items.abstract: The rapid development of artificial intelligence (AI) contrasts with the limited understanding of its economic, organizational, and societal impacts. This paper develops a conceptual model of Hybrid Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence (Hybrid-HCAI), proposing that AI should complement rather than replicate or replace human intelligence. The model integrates three complementary forms of intelligence: subsymbolic AI, symbolic AI, and human intelligence. Subsymbolic AI handles pattern recognition, forecasting, classification, and generation, while symbolic AI represents explicit knowledge, rules, causal relationships, norms, and governance structures. Human intelligence contributes contextual understanding, creativity, intuition, value judgments, social competence, and responsibility. The symbolic layer additionally mediates and regulates interactions between human and machine intelligence, functioning as a “social operating system” for coordination. The paper derives a theoretical impact model focusing on productivity, organizational agility, innovation, structural stability, and cultural integrity. Participation, reciprocity, fairness, trust, and recognition of cognitive contributions serve as key mediators and design variables. The study proposes empirically testable hypotheses and an interdisciplinary research agenda, positioning Hybrid-HCAI as a conceptual research program rather than a validated technology.

items.title: ID2Pattern: Pretraining Generalizable Identity Behavior Patterns for Transaction Risk Foundation Models
items.abstract: Large-scale behavioral pretraining offers a promising route to generalizable representations in online payment systems. However, high-cardinality identity fields such as card, device, and account IDs, though rich in behavioral signals, remain underexploited. Their continually growing vocabularies and limited semantic meaning make existing vocabulary-based and semantics-based encodings ill-suited. Their generalizable signal lies not in specific values, but in the identity behavior patterns they exhibit across a transaction sequence. Building on this insight, we propose ID2Pattern, a pretraining framework that brings these patterns into transaction foundation models. ID2Pattern first encodes identity fields with a Local Anonymous ID (LAID) tokenizer, which captures how each identity appears and recurs within the sequence, independent of its specific value. It then pretrains a multi-scale pattern codebook on unlabeled sequences, which abstracts LAID sequences into discrete behavior patterns for downstream prediction. Experiments on an industrial dataset with over 100M sequences and six public datasets show that ID2Pattern consistently outperforms strong baselines, improving industrial by 4.13% and public datasets by 8.83% on average. Notably, ID2Pattern remains equally effective even when all identity values are unseen during training, highlighting its potential to generalize to new users and markets.

items.title: Impact of AI Technology Proliferation on Internet Security
items.abstract: This conference presentation examines the multifaceted impact of artificial intelligence (AI) proliferation on internet security, cybersecurity practices, software engineering, and digital sovereignty. It considers both the defensive capabilities enabled by AI technologies and the emerging security risks associated with their widespread adoption. The presentation discusses how AI-based solutions can improve cyberattack detection, threat analysis, incident response, and vulnerability identification. At the same time, it highlights the growing potential for malicious applications, including automated malware generation, phishing, deepfakes, social engineering, and disinformation. Particular attention is devoted to security vulnerabilities in AI-driven and agentic systems, including prompt injection, jailbreaking, training data poisoning, goal hijacking, and context manipulation. The analysis addresses the risks associated with excessive system privileges, persistent access to external tools, non-deterministic behavior, and dependencies on untrusted information sources. Security mitigation approaches include static and dynamic application security testing, the principle of least privilege, zero-trust architectures, sandboxed execution, and input/output validation. The presentation also explores the implications of AI-assisted software development, emphasizing the necessity of comprehensive code review, testing, and validation. It identifies potential challenges associated with vibe coding, cognitive debt, declining opportunities for junior developers, and the erosion of organizational knowledge and technical expertise. Broader societal and regulatory considerations include digital sovereignty, technological dependencies, open-source alternatives, responsible AI governance, and emerging European initiatives supporting technological autonomy. The presentation concludes that artificial intelligence can become a strategic asset for cybersecurity when AI models are developed using high-quality data, deployed within appropriate security frameworks, and subjected to effective human oversight and governance.

items.title: Impact of Data Privacy Regulations on Recommender Systems Performance
items.abstract: Data privacy regulations empower consumers to control the collection of their personal data. A significant consequence of these regulations is their effect on various data-driven business solutions, especially on personalization technologies and recommender systems. We investigate the potential impacts of diverse real-world data privacy practices (that can be adopted by firms in response to various data protection regulations) on the recommender systems performance. We also examine how these impacts vary across different personalization contexts and applications. In particular, we distinguish between scenarios where the user population exhibits more stable vs. more dynamic (i.e., changing) preferences, as these scenarios often represent distinctly different recommendation settings. We use a simulation framework, carefully seeded with real-world data, for a comprehensive evaluation of the recommender system performance under numerous scenarios, such as different recommendation algorithms, different data privacy practices, different degrees of users' preference dynamics, etc. Extensive computational experiments uncover several robust performance patterns for different data privacy practices and highlight substantial differences between recommendation settings with stable vs. changing user preferences. Furthermore, building upon the comprehensive findings from our computational experiments, we propose flexible, parameterizable data privacy practice designs based on the notion of revelation protection. The proposed approach is designed to provide an effective balance between personalization performance and privacy considerations, as demonstrated using extensive simulation experiments. The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of privacy-aware recommender systems in the context of contemporary data protection regulations. The findings can also be informative to policymakers for understanding the practical implications of various data privacy practices and for designing future policies.

items.title: Implicit Assumptions About Tasks in Continual Learning
items.abstract: Continual learning is the study of how a model accumulates knowledge from data received over time, rather than all at once. In practice, this is typically achieved by dividing a dataset into tasks and presenting them sequentially. Explanations of the resulting measurements take into account factors such as the similarity between segments, the rate at which the data changes and the order of presentation. Each of these factors can be defined in terms of the underlying data, the partition imposed on it, or the learner that encounters it. These levels do not necessarily coincide, and it is usually left implicit which level a reported quantity refers to. We separate these and identify which properties acquire a value at each level. In controlled teacher--student experiments, we demonstrate that partitioning the same underlying trajectory at different levels of granularity, changing the order of presentation, and varying the similarity structure of the underlying data all result in different measured outcomes. We review representative benchmarks to determine which of these properties are stated. Where the underlying data cannot be inspected, as in foundation models built on undisclosed pre-training corpora, its properties are inherited by the model's initial state, and the training applied on top of it can be described.

items.title: ImplicitHop: Evaluating knowledge integration across context and memory
items.abstract: The ability to integrate new information and deduce its consequences is central to learning, understanding, and reasoning in large language models (LLMs). Whether information arrives during training or in-context, models must not only store local facts, but propagate their long-range implications globally. To explore information integration in LLMs, we introduce two complementary natural language benchmarks for large-scale evaluation of deductive reasoning as a function of inference depth. The first is a formal graph benchmark enabling controlled evaluation over a wide range of graph topologies and integration tasks; the second is a knowledge composition benchmark grounded in real-world knowledge graphs. We use these benchmarks to compare knowledge integration from information encoded in context versus information encoded in model weights during pretraining, evaluating a set of open models implicitly, without chain of thought. We find that accuracy decays sharply with increased composition length for both pretrained and in-context knowledge. Information presented in-context, however, substantially outperforms deduction over information encoded in weights. These results quantify a fundamental limitation of current models with direct implications for prompt-based control of agent behavior and for continual learning strategies, and they provide a foundation for developing training, prompting, and integration methods that support deeper reasoning.
